1415.title: A-L-M
1415.hook: olam, world, and ne'elam, hidden: Hasidic teachers say the world hides God
1415.howItsDone: Hasidic teachers read olam, world, together with he'elem, hiddenness, and teach that the world both conceals God and invites seeking; a Hasidic story tells of a child whose friend stopped looking for him in hide-and-seek.

segments.voice: Yesterday, T-K-N: tikkun, setting right. Your line was fix. A new week of roots begins, and it starts with the word inside tikkun olam.

A small boy runs into his grandfather's study, crying. He'd been playing hide-and-seek. He found a good spot, hid, and waited. And waited. When he finally came out, he found that his friend had stopped looking long ago and wandered off. In the version people tell, the grandfather is a Hasidic rabbi, Rabbi Baruch of Medzhybizh, and when he hears it, he begins to cry too. God says the same thing, he tells the boy. I hide, and no one comes looking.
screen: `A BOY HIDES, AND WAITS.` → `NOBODY IS LOOKING.` → `GOD SAYS THE SAME.`

segments.voice: A-L-M. Ayin, lamed, mem. Olam: world. And ne'elam: hidden. First, time. In the Bible olam can reach toward time more than space: le-olam, forever. A psalm repeats it as a refrain, line after line: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Olam is a stretch so long you can't see its far end. Second, hidden. In Leviticus, a person touches something unclean, "and if it be hidden from him." The Hebrew is ne'lam, from these letters: something real that the person can't see. Third, Kohelet sets the word inside us: God "hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end." The word there is ha-olam, and readers have heard it as the world, or eternity, or something hidden: something vast placed in a person that they can't get to the end of. Fourth, the Hasidic teachers. They read the shared letters as a teaching: the world, olam, is the place where God is ne'elam, hidden. Creation is a kind of hiding place. Notice the difference between hidden and gone. Hidden means someone is there to be found. That's why the grandfather cried.
screen: `OLAM: FOREVER.` · `NE'ELAM: HIDDEN FROM HIM.` · `THE WORLD SET IN THEIR HEART.` · `THE WORLD AS A HIDING PLACE.` · then, large: `HIDDEN IS NOT GONE.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen for the sounds under the obvious ones, a fridge humming, a bird, a car far off, your own breath. Then open them, choose one ordinary object near you, and ask what's hidden in it: the hands that made it, the ground it came from, the road it took to reach you. If you pray, the looking itself can be a kind of seeking; if you don't, let it simply be seeing.
screen: `LISTEN UNDER THE SOUNDS.` · `ONE ORDINARY OBJECT.` · `WHAT'S HIDDEN IN IT?`

Your line: the world hides. A game of hide-and-seek only works if somebody goes looking. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1416.title: G-L-H
1416.hook: galut, exile, and gilui, revealing, share a root
1416.howItsDone: Jewish teaching links galut, exile, and gilui, revealing, through the root gimel-lamed-heh; Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (Jeremiah 29) and the Talmud's teaching that the Shechinah went into exile with Israel (Megillah 29a) can be studied together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-L-M: olam, the world, and ne'elam, hidden. Your line was the world hides. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles first reached you on day eight hundred four; today, a root where hiding turns into showing.

A letter arrives in Babylon from the prophet Jeremiah, addressed to people carried off from Jerusalem. Other prophets have been promising it'll be over soon. Jeremiah tells them to build houses and live in them, plant gardens and eat what grows, marry, raise children. And then this: "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Pray for the city of your exile. The Hebrew under carried away captives is today's root.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `BUILD, PLANT, MARRY.` → `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.`

segments.voice: G-L-H. Gimel, lamed, heh. Galut: exile. Gilui: revealing, uncovering. First, uncovering. The root's plainest sense is to lay something bare. In the book of Ruth, when Boaz wants to tell his relative about Naomi's field, the Hebrew says he wanted to uncover his ear: to let him know. Second, exile. The same letters mean to go into exile, to be carried off. Some readers hear the two meanings as one picture: exile is being uncovered, the covering of home pulled away. Third, God revealed. When Jacob builds an altar at Bethel, the text gives the reason: "because there God appeared unto him, when he fled from the face of his brother." Appeared is from this root, and notice when: while Jacob was running, in his own exile. Deuteronomy draws a line through the root too: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever." The revealed is what's handed to people to live by. Fourth, the rabbis. The Talmud teaches that wherever Israel was exiled, the Shechinah, God's presence, went with them. In this root, being sent away and being shown something share their letters. Jeremiah's letter is itself a revelation, mailed into an exile.
screen: `TO UNCOVER AN EAR.` · `EXILE: THE COVERING PULLED AWAY.` · `GOD APPEARED TO JACOB AS HE FLED.` · `THE PRESENCE WENT INTO EXILE TOO.` · then, large: `EXILE REVEALS.`

segments.voice: Bring back a time you were out of place: a new city, a new school, a hospital stay, a family you married into, a room where nobody spoke your language, and let the strangeness return for a moment. Then ask what it showed you that you couldn't have seen at home, about yourself, about kindness, about what you need, and hold that one thing. If you pray, you can remember Jeremiah's letter and pray for the place you're in now.
screen: `ONE TIME YOU WERE OUT OF PLACE.` · `WHAT DID IT SHOW YOU?` · `HOLD THAT ONE THING.`

segments.voice: G-L-H. Gimel, lamed, heh: galut, exile, and gilui, revealing. To be uncovered, and to be shown. Today's word.
Your line: exile reveals. The Talmud says the presence went into exile too. See you tomorrow.

1417.title: Y-Sh-V
1417.howItsDone: In a yeshiva, students sit for long sessions of Torah study, some of them in pairs; the Shema speaks of the words 'when thou sittest in thine house', and the rabbis prize yishuv ha-da'at, a settled mind, before learning or deciding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, G-L-H: galut, exile, and gilui, revealing. Your line was exile reveals. You visited the great yeshivas of Babylonia on day nine hundred nine; today, after all that moving, the root for sitting down.

Two brothers, described in a single verse. "Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents." One goes out. One stays in. The Hebrew for dwelling there is yoshev: sitting. The rabbis didn't let that word pass. In the midrash, and in Rashi after it, Jacob's tents become tents of study, and the quiet brother becomes a man sitting over his learning. Not much happens in that half of the verse. A man sits. Today's root is the one under his seat, and under the word yeshiva.
screen: `A HUNTER, A MAN OF THE FIELD.` → `A PLAIN MAN, DWELLING IN TENTS.` → `TENTS OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: Y-Sh-V. Yod, shin, vet. Yashav: to sit, to dwell, to settle. First, the yeshiva, the house of Torah study. The word is a sitting, a session: learning is something you do by staying put long enough. Second, the Shema. It says to speak these words "when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way." Sitting at home comes first in the list: the chair, the table, the ordinary evening. Third, where you sit, and with whom. The first psalm blesses the one who walks not in the counsel of the ungodly, "nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful." Sitteth is yashav; seat is moshav, from the same letters. And another psalm sings, "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" Dwell there is shevet, sitting. The root cares about the company you keep in your chair. Fourth, settling. Yishuv is a settlement, a place people have put down roots. And the rabbis speak of yishuv ha-da'at, a settled mind: the calm that lets a person think clearly before deciding. The same letters cover a village on a hillside and a mind that has stopped racing. So the root makes an offer that sounds almost too simple. Sit down. Stay. Let your thoughts land. Then learn something, sitting where you are.
screen: `YESHIVA: A SITTING.` · `WHEN THOU SITTEST IN THINE HOUSE.` · `NOR SITTETH IN THE SEAT OF THE SCORNFUL.` · `YISHUV HA-DA'AT: A SETTLED MIND.` · then, large: `SIT DOWN. STAY. LEARN.`

segments.voice: Feel your seat hold you, feet on the floor, and let your thoughts land one at a time. Then say one line slowly, perhaps the Shema's when thou sittest in thine house, and stay with it word by word without hurrying to the end; if a question comes, set it aside, it'll keep. If you pray, the line can be your prayer.

1418.title: Ch-V-R
1418.hook: chaver, chavruta: friend, study partner, joining
1418.howItsDone: In a traditional beit midrash, students learn in chavruta, pairs who read the text aloud and question each other; Pirkei Avot teaches 'acquire for yourself a friend', and the Talmud's saying 'either companionship or death' comes from the story of Choni.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Y-Sh-V: yashav, to sit, to dwell, to settle. Your line was sit and learn. Learning in pairs had its own day back on day one hundred fifty-one; today, the person sitting across from you.

The sound reaches you first: a big room full of voices, and nobody quiet. People sit in pairs over open books, reading a line out loud, pointing, arguing, asking each other what it means and then asking again. Nobody is lecturing. Somebody laughs; somebody slaps the table. In a traditional study hall, this is what learning can sound like. Each pair is a chavruta. Each partner is a chaver. Today's root is the one that ties them together.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF VOICES.` → `PAIRS OVER OPEN BOOKS.` → `CHAVRUTA.`

segments.voice: Ch-V-R. Chet, vet, resh. To join, to connect. A chaver is a friend, a companion; a chavruta, a study partnership. First, joining. When the tabernacle is built, its curtains are "coupled together one to another," and the Hebrew uses this root. A psalm calls Jerusalem "a city that is compact together," joined to itself: the same letters again. A friend, in this root, is someone you're fastened to. Second, choosing. The sayings of the fathers teach: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire for yourself a friend. A teacher you appoint. A friend, the Hebrew says, you acquire, as if it costs you something. Third, the hard story. The Talmud tells of Choni, who slept for seventy years. He wakes and goes to the study hall, and hears the scholars saying how clear the teaching used to be in Choni's day. He tells them who he is. They don't believe him, and don't give him the honor due. Heartbroken, he prays for mercy and dies. And the sage Rava says: this is why people say, o chavruta o mituta. Either companionship, or death. Fourth, the pair. That's the weight a study partner carries. Your chaver catches what you missed, pushes back, asks the question you were avoiding. In this root, a friend isn't a spectator to your life. A friend is joined to the work.
screen: `CURTAINS COUPLED TOGETHER.` · `ACQUIRE YOURSELF A FRIEND.` · `CHONI, UNRECOGNIZED.` · `EITHER COMPANIONSHIP, OR DEATH.` · then, large: `A FRIEND IS JOINED TO THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Bring one friend to mind, someone you'd call if something went wrong, or someone you've drifted from, and remember one thing you know because of them: a skill, a habit, a way of seeing. Then think of one small way to join them, a call, a walk, a page you could read together, and if you pray, pray for them by name. If loneliness ever feels too heavy to carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
screen: `ONE FRIEND.` · `ONE THING YOU KNOW BECAUSE OF THEM.` · `ONE WAY TO JOIN THEM.`

1419.title: Sh-Ch-R
1419.hook: shachar, dawn; Shacharit, the morning prayer
1419.howItsDone: Shacharit, the morning service, is prayed each day from dawn; it opens with the morning blessings, including thanks for the rooster's understanding to tell day from night, and the Talmud links it to Abraham rising early (Berakhot 26b).

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ch-V-R: chaver, a friend, and chavruta, a study pair. Your line was friendship joins. Today, the first light.

All night, beside a river, Jacob wrestles with a stranger. The stranger can't overcome him. Jacob is hurt, but he won't let go. Then the stranger says, "Let me go, for the day breaketh." In Hebrew, ki alah ha-shachar: for the dawn has come up. And Jacob answers, "I will not let thee go, except thou bless me." The night is ending, and the first light is the thing the stranger can't stay for. Today's root is the word for that light.
screen: `ALL NIGHT BY THE RIVER.` → `LET ME GO, FOR THE DAY BREAKETH.` → `NOT WITHOUT A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Sh-Ch-R. Shin, chet, resh. Shachar: dawn, the first light. First, a psalm that gets up before the sun: "Awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early." The Hebrew is a'irah shachar, which can also be read: I will wake the dawn. Not waiting for morning to wake you; going out to wake it. Second, another psalm asks where a person could go to get away from God's presence: "If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; even there shall thy hand lead me." The wings of the morning are kanfei shachar, the dawn's wings. As far and as fast as light can run, and still held. Third, the prayer. The morning service is Shacharit, the dawn prayer. The Talmud gives two views of where the daily prayers come from. One says the patriarchs established them, and gives the morning to Abraham, from a verse: "Abraham gat up early in the morning to the place where he stood before the LORD." The other ties the prayers to the daily offerings in the Temple. Fourth, the line itself. Among the morning blessings is one that thanks God for giving the rooster understanding to tell day from night. Dawn is a line drawn slowly across the sky, and the tradition meets it with words.
screen: `I WILL WAKE THE DAWN.` · `THE WINGS OF THE MORNING.` · `SHACHARIT: ABRAHAM ROSE EARLY.` · `THE ROOSTER TELLS DAY FROM NIGHT.` · then, large: `MEET THE FIRST LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If it's morning, turn toward a window; if it's later, find the brightest light near you, or close your eyes and remember the last sunrise you saw. Look for the edge where light meets shadow, on a wall, the floor, the side of your hand, and watch it while your breathing slows. If you pray, you can say the psalm's words: I myself will awake early.
screen: `TURN TOWARD THE LIGHT.` · `FIND THE EDGE OF IT.` · `WATCH.`

1420.title: A-R-V
1420.hook: erev, evening; arev, sweet, and a guarantor: all Israel are guarantors
1420.howItsDone: Jewish days, Shabbat and festivals begin at evening, read from Genesis 1:5; the blessing before Torah study asks that its words be sweet; and the Talmud's principle 'all Israel are guarantors for one another' (Shevuot 39a) is cited for mutual responsibility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-Ch-R: shachar, the first light, and Shacharit, the morning prayer. Your line was dawn. On day one thousand two hundred forty-nine you met all Israel responsible for one another; today, the root inside that line, and the other end of the day.

A father refuses to send his youngest son down to Egypt. He has already lost one boy; he won't risk Benjamin. But the family is running out of food. Then Judah, an older brother, steps forward: "I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him." Put him on my account. If he doesn't come back, the blame is mine. Later, in Egypt, when Benjamin is about to be kept as a slave, Judah steps forward again and offers to stay in his place. Today's root is the word under surety.
screen: `A FATHER WON'T SEND BENJAMIN.` → `I WILL BE SURETY FOR HIM.` → `LET ME STAY INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: A-R-V. Ayin, resh, vet. These letters carry more than one meaning. First, evening: erev. The Torah's first day ends with it: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Evening is named before morning, and the rabbis read that as the reason a Jewish day, Shabbat included, begins in the evening. Second, sweet: arev. A psalm says, "My meditation of him shall be sweet." And the blessing said before studying Torah asks God to make its words sweet in our mouths, with a word from these letters. Third, the guarantor: arev again, the one who stands surety, the way Judah did for his brother. The Talmud puts it in a single line: kol Yisrael arevim zeh ba-zeh, all Israel are guarantors for one another. In its setting it explains how one person can bear responsibility for another's wrong. In its widest reading it says that nobody in the community is only on their own account. Fourth, side by side. These may be separate words that happen to share a spelling. Some teachers set them together anyway: a day that begins in the dark, words that taste sweet, and people who answer for each other. Judah's surety is where it gets concrete. He didn't promise to feel responsible. He put himself in the place where Benjamin would have stood.
screen: `EREV: EVENING COMES FIRST.` · `AREV: SWEET IN THE MOUTH.` · `AREV: THE ONE WHO STANDS SURETY.` · `ALL ISRAEL ARE GUARANTORS.` · then, large: `WE STAND SURETY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person whose life touches yours, a child, a parent, a coworker who's struggling, a friend who's gone quiet, and see yourself standing beside them, the way Judah stood beside his brother. Ask where you could put your name beside theirs, vouching for them, going with them to a hard appointment, speaking up for them in a room they aren't in, and hold that in mind. 1421.title: N-S-A
1421.hook: nasa: to lift, to carry, as in Naso
1421.howItsDone: The Torah portion Naso (Numbers 4:21–7:89) takes its name from 'naso et rosh', lift up the head; it includes the priestly blessing, which the priests give with raised hands, nesiat kapayim. Exodus 34:7 uses the same verb for forgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-R-V: erev, evening, and arev, the one who stands surety. Your line was we stand surety. The priestly blessing had its own day back on day four hundred thirty-nine; today's root does its lifting.

When the Torah counts people, it doesn't always use a word for counting. In the portion called Naso, God tells Moses: "Take also the sum of the sons of Gershon." The Hebrew is naso et rosh: lift up the head. To count someone, in that phrasing, is to raise their head, to see each face, one at a time. Later in the same portion comes a blessing that lifts something else: "The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Today's root does the lifting in both.
screen: `NASO: LIFT UP THE HEAD.` → `EACH FACE, ONE AT A TIME.` → `LIFT UP HIS COUNTENANCE.`

segments.voice: N-S-A. Nun, sin, alef. Nasa: to lift, to carry, to bear. First, the eyes. "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." I will lift is essa, from this root. Lifting begins with where you look. Second, the shoulders. In the same portion, Naso, the Levites of Kohath carry the holy things of the sanctuary, and the text says they bore them upon their shoulders: the same verb. The leaders of the tribes in that portion are called nesi'im, from these letters too. Third, forgiveness. When God's attributes are proclaimed to Moses, one of them is "forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin." The Hebrew for forgiving there is nosei: carrying. To forgive, in this root, is to lift a wrong off someone and bear it. Cain uses the same verb from the other side, in despair: "My punishment is greater than I can bear." Too heavy to lift. Fourth, the hands. When the priests bless the people with the words from Naso, the practice is called nesiat kapayim, the lifting of the hands. So one root raises heads to be counted, eyes to the hills, holy things onto shoulders, wrongs off backs, and hands in blessing. In this root, lifting and carrying and forgiving are one motion.

segments.voice: Let your shoulders rise on an in-breath and drop on the out-breath, a few times, slowly. Then ask what someone near you is carrying that you could lift a little, a chore, a worry, a grudge you could set down, or choose a weight of your own to put down for now. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills. And if something ever feels too heavy to bear alone, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, any hour; elsewhere, local emergency help.
